These data likely arise mostly from CE-CERT because they had over 50 hours of data tracked in early morning hours on these roadways, whereas FleetDNA had about 5 hours. Again, this peak just under 60 mph may be due to service vehicles such as freeway work trucks, street sweepers, or towing trucks performing their functions on these roadways rather than just driving freely. The data density for these hours is relatively good, but to exercise caution toward hours with more data, hour IDs 1 and 2 could possibly be replaced with hour ID 3 and hour IDs 22–24 replaced with the distribution from hour ID 21. For late morning and afternoon hours of the day, we see the more common 60-mph peak in distribution on urban freeways. We observe a similar trend on weekends, with slightly more time spent at lower speeds such as 20 mph. As we see in the average speeds section, hour IDs 1–4 and 15–24 have more uncertainty, and if urban freeway weekend data were used, hour ID 14 could possibly substitute for the night hours containing less data, and similarly hour ID 5 for the early morning hours. For urban other roads, we see them spending about 25% of their time at the 10-mph speed bin, and less time up until about 40 mph, above which the distribution nearly hits zero. In hours near midnight, we see trucks driving less between 10–20 mph and more at 50–60 mph. Despite aggregating data from two different data sets, rural roads still only contain a few hours of data per hour ID. As usual, we see some preference for higher speeds on freeways and lower speeds on other roads, but results are much more variable on rural roads. With possible minor edits to urban freeways on weekdays, and if major edits are made as described for urban freeways on weekends, all hours of urban driving could reflect these updated speed distributions. Figure 36. Combined speed bin distributions for single-unit short-haul vehicles by hour Figure 37 shows the speed bin distributions for refuse trucks from both data sets. On urban freeways on weekdays, we see the characteristic 60-mph peak, which is more pronounced for late night and early morning hours. For midday and afternoon hours, trucks spent proportionally less time at 60 mph and more under 40 mph, with a minor peak at 5 mph, possibly due to more vehicles on the road during these hours.
